extracted.intended_audience: People of the State of New York; citizens and readers interested in constitutional design and the federal judiciary
extracted.subtask_description: Principles and standards for structuring and evaluating the federal judiciary: its proper objects/jurisdiction, the role of courts in interpreting the Constitution, and institutional safeguards for judicial independence and responsibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Supremacy of the Constitution / judicial review
rubrics_metrics.description: Every act of a delegated authority, contrary to the tenor of the commission under which it is exercised, is void. No legislative act, therefore, contrary to the Constitution, can be valid.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts ascertain the meaning of the Constitution and must prefer it over inconsistent statutes; to deny this would make representatives superior to the people. This doctrine underpins the courts' power to declare statutes void when they contravene the Constitution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpretation of the laws is the province of the courts
rubrics_metrics.description: The interpretation of the laws is the proper and peculiar province of the courts. A constitution is, in fact, and must be regarded by the judges, as a fundamental law.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts are conceived as an intermediate body between the people and the legislature to keep the latter within its assigned authority; judges are the appropriate actors to ascertain meaning of constitutional and statutory provisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rule for resolving conflicts between statutes (equal authorities)
rubrics_metrics.description: Where two statutes clash and neither contains a repealing clause, the rule which has obtained in the courts is that the last in order of time shall be preferred to the first.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a rule of construction adopted by courts (not a positive law) based on reason and propriety; it applies between interfering acts of an equal authority.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rule for resolving conflicts between superior and subordinate authority
rubrics_metrics.description: In regard to the interfering acts of a superior and subordinate authority ... the prior act of a superior ought to be preferred to the subsequent act of an inferior and subordinate authority.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When a subordinate statute contravenes a superior (e.g., constitutional) provision, courts should adhere to the superior provision and disregard the subordinate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Permanency of judicial tenure (good behavior)
rubrics_metrics.description: Next to permanency in office, nothing can contribute more to the independence of the judges ... the convention acted wisely in copying from the models of those constitutions which have established GOOD BEHAVIOR as the tenure of their judicial offices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Permanent tenure (during good behaviour) secures judicial independence against legislative or executive influence and encourages the integrity and impartiality necessary for protecting constitutional and individual rights.

rubrics_metrics.name: Protection of judicial compensation (not diminished)
rubrics_metrics.description: The plan ... has provided that the judges of the United States 'shall at STATED TIMES receive for their services a compensation which shall not be DIMINISHED during their continuance in office.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Protecting judges' salaries from diminution prevents legislative power over subsistence from becoming power over will; allowing increases accommodates changes in value of money while preventing financial punishment or coercion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Impeachment as the safeguard for judicial responsibility
rubrics_metrics.description: The precautions for their responsibility are comprised in the article respecting impeachments. They are liable to be impeached for malconduct by the House of Representatives, and tried by the Senate; and, if convicted, may be dismissed from office, and disqualified for holding any other.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Impeachment is the prescribed mechanism to hold judges accountable for misconduct while preserving independence from ordinary political pressures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Against removal for inability / age limits as poor safeguard
rubrics_metrics.description: The want of a provision for removing the judges on account of inability has been a subject of complaint. But ... such a provision would either not be practiced upon or would be more liable to abuse than calculated to answer any good purpose.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measuring mental faculties is unreliable; categorical age limits (e.g., New York's age 60) are criticized as inapt and inhumane. Except for clear insanity, removal for 'inability' risks arbitrary or partisan abuse.

rubrics_metrics.name: Need for legal learning, precedents, and integrity in judges
rubrics_metrics.description: A voluminous code of laws ... the records of those precedents must unavoidably swell to a very considerable bulk, and must demand long and laborious study to acquire a competent knowledge of them. Hence it is, that there can be but few men in the society who will have sufficient skill in the laws to qualify them for the stations of judges.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judicial office requires exceptional learning and integrity; permanent tenure is necessary to attract and retain such qualified individuals and to justify the long study required to apply precedent and strict rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Single Supreme Court of final jurisdiction (distinct body)
rubrics_metrics.description: There ought to be one court of supreme and final jurisdiction ... The only question that seems to have been raised concerning it, is, whether it ought to be a distinct body or a branch of the legislature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A distinct Supreme Court is preferred to vesting ultimate decision in a legislative branch because legislators lack the specialized knowledge and independence required to correct or moderate laws they helped make.

rubrics_metrics.name: Judicial power coextensive with legislative power for uniformity
rubrics_metrics.description: If there are such things as political axioms, the propriety of the judicial power of a government being coextensive with its legislative, may be ranked among the number. The mere necessity of uniformity in the interpretation of the national laws, decides the question.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Federal courts should have jurisdiction adequate to give efficacy to constitutional provisions and to secure uniform interpretation of national laws; multiple independent final courts would produce contradiction and confusion.

rubrics_metrics.name: First: Jurisdiction — cases in law and equity arising under the Constitution and laws of the United States
rubrics_metrics.description: First. To all cases in law and equity, ARISING UNDER THE CONSTITUTION and THE LAWS OF THE UNITED STATES.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Includes constitutional prohibitions on states (e.g., emission of paper money). Equitable jurisdiction is necessary where fraud, trust, hardship, or cross-state land-grant disputes arise, especially when foreigners are involved.

rubrics_metrics.name: Second: Jurisdiction — treaties and cases affecting ambassadors and public ministers
rubrics_metrics.description: Second. To treaties made, or which shall be made, under the authority of the United States, and to all cases affecting ambassadors, other public ministers, and consuls.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These matters relate to preservation of national peace and international obligations and therefore belong to national tribunals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Third: Jurisdiction — admiralty and maritime causes
rubrics_metrics.description: Third. To cases of admiralty and maritime jurisdiction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maritime causes commonly depend on the laws of nations and affect rights of foreigners; federal cognizance of these is reasonable and established.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fourth: Jurisdiction — controversies to which the United States shall be a party
rubrics_metrics.description: Fourth. To controversies to which the United States shall be a party.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Controversies involving the nation and its members/citizens must be referred to national tribunals for proper adjudication.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fifth: Jurisdiction — controversies involving interstate relations and peace of Confederacy
rubrics_metrics.description: Fifth. To controversies between two or more States; between a State and citizens of another State; between citizens of different States.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Federal courts must resolve causes affecting the peace of the whole (intercourse between states or with foreign nations) to avoid devolving the peace of the Union to a single part.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sixth: Jurisdiction — citizens of the same State claiming lands under different State grants
rubrics_metrics.description: Sixth. To cases between the citizens of the same State, CLAIMING LANDS UNDER GRANTS OF DIFFERENT STATES.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These are specifically contemplated instances where federal judicial cognizance is necessary because local courts may be biased or laws pre-judge the questions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Seventh: Jurisdiction — cases between a State (or its citizens) and foreign states or citizens
rubrics_metrics.description: Seventh. To cases between a State and the citizens thereof, and foreign States, citizens, or subjects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To preserve public faith and foreign relations, such disputes are appropriately within national judicature; federal courts, lacking local attachments, are likelier to be impartial.

rubrics_metrics.name: Federal jurisdiction where State tribunals cannot be impartial
rubrics_metrics.description: The reasonableness of the agency of the national courts in cases in which the State tribunals cannot be supposed to be impartial, speaks for itself. No man ought certainly to be a judge in his own cause.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where state courts have interests or biases (e.g., land grants favoring the State), federal tribunals should preside to ensure impartiality and fairness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Necessity of equitable jurisdiction in federal courts
rubrics_metrics.description: What equitable causes can grow out of the Constitution and laws of the United States? ... There is hardly a subject of litigation between individuals, which may not involve those ingredients of FRAUD, ACCIDENT, TRUST, or HARDSHIP, which would render the matter an object of equitable rather than of legal jurisdiction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Federal courts must have equity powers to relieve against unconscionable bargains and to resolve disputes (e.g., cross-state land conveyances) where legal remedies are insufficient, particularly when foreigners are concerned.
